question.text:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

  1. $\mathbf{T}_1 : \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $\mathbf{T}_2 : \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2 \end{bmatrix}$
  3. $\mathbf{T}_3 : \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7 \end{bmatrix}$
question.explanation:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form \[ \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b, \] where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $\det(A) \neq 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_1$ is not invertible. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_1$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 6u+3v \\ 10u+5v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*} Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get \[ \det(A) = \left| \begin{matrix} 6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5 \end{matrix} \right| = 5 \cdot 6 - 3 \cdot 10 = 0. \] Since the determinant is zero, $\mathbf T_1$ is not invertible.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_2$ is not invertible. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_2$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -3u-4v \\ 3u+4v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*} Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get \[ \det(A) = \left| \begin{matrix} -3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4 \end{matrix} \right| = 4 \cdot (-3) - (-4) \cdot 3 = 0. \] Since the determinant is zero, $\mathbf T_2$ is not invertible.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_3$ is invertible. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_3$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -6u-4v \\ 8u+7v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -7 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -7 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*} Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get \[ \det(A) = \left| \begin{matrix} -6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7 \end{matrix} \right| = 7 \cdot (-6) - (-4) \cdot 8 = -10 \neq 0. \] Since the determinant is nonzero, $\mathbf T_3$ is invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\mathbf{T}_3$ only."

question.text:
Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ defined as

\[ x = 4u + 2v - 5, \qquad y = 2u + v + 6. \]

Suppose that $A$ is the matrix that represents the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -5 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $\det(A) = 0$
  3. The transformation is invertible
question.explanation:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form \[ \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b, \] where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

  • Statement I is false. The given transformation can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 4u + 2v - 5 \\ 2u + v + 6 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4u + 2v \\ 2u + v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*} Therefore, \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \neq \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -5 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • Statement II is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get \[ \det(A) = \left| \begin{matrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{matrix} \right| = 1 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 2 = 0. \]

  • Statement III is false. Since $\det(A) = 0,$ the affine transformation is not invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

\[ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -5 \\ -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}+ \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is given by

\[ \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{a} & 5 \\ \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{b} & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{c} \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form \[ \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b, \] where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $\mathbf{T},$ we get

\begin{align*} A\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b} &= \mathbf{x} \\[5pt] A\mathbf{u} &= \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] \mathbf{u} &= A^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}). \end{align*}

The matrix form of $\mathbf T$ gives us the following information:

\[ \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 7 & -5 \\ -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b} \]

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A{:}$

\begin{align*} A^{-1} &= \dfrac{1}{3 \cdot 7 - (-5) \cdot (4)}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Therefore, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

\begin{align*} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}}_{A^{-1}} \cdot \Bigg( \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf x} - \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b} \Bigg) \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{3} & 5 \\ \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{4} & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{3} \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \[ a+b+c = 3 + 4 + 3 = 10. \]

  • If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

  • If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases:

    • If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

    • If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf{T}$ is a zero matrix $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. $

Therefore, $\mathbf{T}$ is non-invertible, and the image of the triangle under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a point on the plane.

question.text: Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by \[ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ -2 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}. \] What would be the image of the pentagon shown above under the action of $\mathbf{T}?$
question.explanation:
Recall that for any affine transformation \[ \mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b}, \] where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

  • If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

  • If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases:

    • If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

    • If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf{T}$ is $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ -2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. $

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} \det(T) &= \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ -2 & -4 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 3\cdot (-4) - (-2) \cdot 6 \\[5pt] &= 0. \end{align*}

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix.

Therefore, $\mathbf{T}$ is non-invertible, and the image of the pentagon under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a line segment.

question.text: Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by \[ x = 3u-v-1, \qquad y = 2u+5v. \] What would be the image of the rectangle shown above under the action of $\mathbf{T}?$
question.explanation:
Recall that for any affine transformation \[ \mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b}, \] where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

  • If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

  • If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases:

    • If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

    • If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

The given transformation can be expressed as

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 3u -v-1 \\ 2u +5v \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3u -v \\ 2u+5v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 2 &5 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf{T}$ is $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3& -1 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}. $

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} \det(T) &= \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 3 \cdot 5 - 2 \cdot (-1) \\[5pt] &= 17 \\[5pt] &\neq 0. \end{align*}

So, we have a non-singular matrix.

Therefore, $\mathbf{T}$ is invertible, and the image of the rectangle under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a parallelogram.
